questions.question: Describe the characteristics of South African unemployment and explain why growth alone will not clear it.
questions.expected_answer: It is structural rather than merely cyclical (persisting through upswings); youth-concentrated, with first-time seekers waiting longest; skill-divided, falling steeply as education rises; spatially uneven, heaviest in former homeland areas and townships far from economic centres; long-term, with a large share jobless a year or more, eroding skills, networks and confidence; and carrying a large discouragement margin, so the expanded rate exceeds the strict one. Growth alone is insufficient because capital-intensive or skill-concentrated growth can raise output while bypassing the unskilled — and remedies must reach people the market currently bypasses entirely.

questions.question: Distinguish the types of unemployment with an example and remedy for each.
questions.expected_answer: Frictional: people between jobs (the graduate searching for a first post) — short-term and normal; remedied by information and job-matching services. Structural: a mismatch of skills or locations (the retrenched mineworker whose skills fit no growing sector; the willing worker two hours from the jobs) — South Africa's dominant type; remedied by education, artisan and technical training, retraining and spatial measures. Cyclical: caused by the downswing (retrenchments when orders dry up); remedied by demand — state spending, lower interest rates, export growth. Seasonal: work existing only part of the year (harvest, holiday retail); remedied by diversification and off-season work or training. Technological: machines replacing tasks; remedied like structural, by retraining toward the work technology creates.

questions.question: Evaluate the three approaches to solving unemployment, giving strengths and limits of each.
questions.expected_answer: Growth of production: derived demand means more output needs more labour — strongest because the jobs are sustainable and self-financing, especially where growth favours labour-intensive sectors, SMEs and exports; limited because capital-intensive growth can raise output without employment. Public works programmes (e.g. the EPWP): the state employs people directly — immediate income, first work experience and lasting assets; limited because jobs are temporary and modestly paid, funded from the budget at an opportunity cost, and must lead to training or further work — a bridge, not a destination. Unemployment insurance (the UIF, funded 1% each from employee and employer): cushions the income shock, prevents destitution during search and stabilises spending in downswings; limited because benefits are temporary and partial, and only former formal employees qualify — excluding the never-employed young, the largest group. The conclusion: diagnose the type before prescribing; no single instrument solves a structural problem.
